cells.tense: You are at the bench with the pen in hand, making the pass you are on and no further.
cells.act: sort what matters from what does not, carefully
cells.ask: Look back over a week of the work and sort what actually built something from what only kept you busy. Cross one item off the second pile for good. Nothing else changes.
cells.core:
You can put your whole attention on the work at hand — one pass, then the next — and the passes stack up on their own. When this sits right, that is what it looks like: you show up, you go a little deeper than last time, and you don't spend the session auditing whether the whole thing is worth it. The hours are quiet, and the quiet isn't lonely. It is where the skill lives.
The part worth tending is what those hours go to. You are far enough in that not every session pays the same, and a day can slide toward the piece that is easy to touch instead of the piece that would sharpen you. Once this week, sort what you did and cross off one thing that didn't build anything. The rest of the list stays yours.
cells.sheetLine: You go deeper each pass because you keep showing up.
cells.verb: building a craft deeper with each pass at it
cells.place: at the bench where you aim your own attention

cells.tense: You are running past the work, bracing for the version of it that is not built yet.
cells.act: share the joy with the people it belongs to
cells.ask: Take something you finished, however small, and tell someone who would be glad about it, out loud, with the gladness still on it. Before the next piece starts.
cells.core:
You know how to keep at something until it gets good, and the getting-good part is being rushed. The next stage is already running in your head while your hands are still on this one, and the plan keeps growing longer than the week can hold. From outside it reads as urgency. At the bench it feels like pressure that doesn't give the work room to breathe.
What the work is short on isn't hours. It is the other half of the deal, where something gets to be finished and enjoyed before you move on. So take one finished thing, even a small piece of it, to someone who would be glad, and say what it is and let yourself like it while they hear it. The unfinished thing stays where it is, and you will come back to it looser.

cells.tense: The time you kept at this is behind you, and you are standing where it left you.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Say out loud what this work is for — its shape, what it does — to whoever is around it, before they ask. One sentence. Yours to claim.
cells.core:
You have put real time into this, and the time is real, and somewhere along the way you stopped saying what it is for. You keep it private, you don't mention that you are building it, and when someone asks you go vague or change the subject. So the thing almost doesn't count, even to you.
The work doesn't know you have gone quiet about it. It just doesn't get claimed. Try this: take the version of it you would say to a stranger, the one that actually fits the thing, and say it to whoever is around it before they ask. Not to sell it. To give it a shape that includes you. You may find the sentence runs longer than expected, and steadies as it goes.

cells.tense: You are already at the bench writing the next pass, and you would say the hand moved on its own.
cells.act: let the will and the wanting go the same way
cells.ask: Before the next pass, pause and check whether you actually want to be at the bench today. If yes, the hour is yours. If no, set the pen down and do something else. Either answer is real.
cells.core:
The work is moving, and there is a hand on it, and if asked you would say it just needed doing. Some part of you keeps this going — showing up, choosing the direction, holding the line — and none of that gets filed as a choice you made. It gets filed under what the thing required. That is the part that tires a person quietly.
Here is something small. Next time you go to the bench, don't move yet — check first whether you want to be there. If the answer is yes, the hour is yours and you will know it. If the answer is no, set it down or spend the hour elsewhere, and that stands on its own as an answer. The commitment stays; you get to be the one holding it.
cells.sheetLine: The work moves because you keep choosing it, and you do not count it.
cells.verb: building a craft deeper with each pass at it
